newsitem.title: INDIA: Illegal Indian Gulf workers return to harsh reality.
newsitem.headline: Illegal Indian Gulf workers return to harsh reality.

text.p: More than 1,800 Indian workers, expelled by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and other Gulf states, disembarked from a passenger ship in Bombay on Monday while another vessel carrying 1,200 waited offshore.
Bombay port officials said the Al Madina was the first ship to bring home such a large number since the crackdown on illegal immigrant workers in the UAE, Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
They said the Sea Wolf, a cargo vessel carrying about 1,200 illegal workers, also arrived in Bombay harbour Monday and would dock on Tuesday.
Crowded on the deck of the Al Madina, the illegal workers looked dishevelled as they clutched small cloth bundles and awaited their turn to disembark.
"This is the first time I have seen such a pathetic sight," said an immigration official as he guided the returnees in a single file into a large, makeshift immigration hall.
"Most of these people have no passports. They only have emergency certificates, issued by Indian authorities in the Emirates," the official said.
Tales of harship abounded. "I was in jail in Jeddah for 15 days before I was put on the ship," said Amir Ahmed, 23, an electrician, who broke down while describing his plight.
Ahmed left his native south Indian state of Kerala a few months ago for Saudi Arabia to find work -- but without the necessary papers.
He was one of 1,823 illegal Indian workers returning on the Al Madina, which was chartered by Indian Embassy authorities in the UAE to bring them back.
Sheikh Rahim Basha, a tailor from southern Andhra Pradesh state, said he lost his passport in the UAE. He was given an emergency certificate and put on the ship.
"I worked for eight months and took salary for five months which was just enough for food and accommodation. My three months' salary is still due. But I had to leave," Basha said.
"Only mindless people go to the Gulf leaving their own country." he added. "I need 320 rupees to go to my village from here. But I don't have a single rupee."

Police took into protective custody two children, Sadiqul Alam, 8, and Hussain, 7, who said they had been taken by their fathers to Jeddah where they sold water to make money. They did not know what had happened to their fathers.
"These kids will be sent to their homes in Calcutta," said a police official.
Most of the returning workers complained of harassment by the ship's crew.
"We were beaten up when we asked for food," said Nanda Kumar, a worker from Kerala. "The crew is against people from Kerala. We had undergone so much difficulty, god alone knows."
Local agents for the Al Madina denied the charges that passengers had been ill-treated.
"We are transporting these people out of the dockyard by buses. Our responsibility ends at that," said Captain J.D. Shroff, Bombay agent for the Al Madina.
Shroff said the ship would make another three trips to the Gulf port of Sharja to bring back at least 6,000 more workers expelled workers from the UAE in the next few days.
Officials in the Kerala capital of Trivandrum have estimated the number of workers returning to the state at around 30,000.
